comments.author: @ScottfromNB
comments.text: I grew up on the Bay of Fundy coast just west of Saint John at Duck Cove. Over 20 years from 1956 to 1976, I watched the edge of the gravel/sand bluff over Duck Cove recede over 20 feet, taking at least 5 summer homes over the cliff with it. Once down on the beach below, all evidence of them disappeared in a couple of years. Sadly, such locations, common on both the Bay of Fundy and the east coast of New Brunswick would've been a prime site for Indigenous settlements, even for the never located "Vineland" Viking settlement, possibly on the Gulf of St. Lawrence side of NB. Any evidence of them would be long gone like the summer homes that disappeared when I was a kid.

replies.author: @HiddenCanada
replies.text: That’s not what the evidence shows. The oldest confirmed human sites in New Brunswick date back roughly 12,700 years, while the earliest confirmed European presence in North America is the Norse site at L’Anse aux Meadows from around AD 1000, more than 11,000 years later. And even at L’Anse aux Meadows, Indigenous peoples had used the area thousands of years before the Norse arrived. Archaeology doesn’t support the claim that Europeans were here first.
